newsitem.title: UK: Tighter internal controls needed in metals - Becke.
newsitem.headline: Tighter internal controls needed in metals - Becke.

text.p: Tighter internal controls are needed within the metals industry, otherwise the London Metal Exchange (LME) will be pushed further into regulatory hands, metals consultant Wolfgang Becker said.

"Generally, more responsibility must be put on those using the instruments rather than those providing them," Becker, a former trader with Iceni, Metallgesellschaft, Merrill Lynch and Shearson said in the latest issue of the trade publication Metal Bulletin.
Becker was commenting on crisis events in the metals market, mostly in copper, which becomes distorted with erratic price movements and unexpected backwardations.
In mid-1996, the Sumitomo Corp scandal erupted, when the Japanese company fired its head trader Yasuo Hamanaka, alleging he was a rogue who ran up losses of $2.6 billion in unauthorised trading.
Hamanaka is now on trial in Tokyo for fraud and forgery, while investigations are underway in the U.K. and the U.S.
Becker said the LME and the regulators have so far done a good job, but queried whether there are sufficient controlling instruments available with the user.

"By now there has been enough publicity outlining the reasons for the various recent incidents, and therefore no corporation, wherever it is located, should ever look to blame the outside world for its own internal problems again," he said.
The LME and regulatory roles are clearly defined, and they cannot be made responsible for individuals who do not know how to handle the available tools.

"Failure to implement such controls and risk management will push the LME more and more into the hands of the regulators, some of which seem to be doing more than providing a safety net which is still permeable enough to let through enough business to allow the market to function properly," Becker said.
Over-regulation, which would result from any future disasters would mean greater volatility and less volume.
It would also probably support the creation of a secondary market which would be in the hands of a few powerful players at whose mercy the traditional hedger would end up, he added.
